result:
**Words That Happen Once**

There's a term philologists use for a word that appears exactly once in a given body of text: *hapax legomenon*. Said once. The plural is *hapax legomena*, which sounds like a species of moth.

Every large corpus has them, and there are more than you'd think. A surprising fraction of any vocabulary consists of words that show up a single time and then never again — not because they're exotic, usually, but because that's just how word frequency works. A few words do the heavy lifting (*the*, *and*, *of*), and then there's an enormous tail of things said once and dropped.

Most of the time this doesn't matter. But it matters intensely when the corpus is closed — when no more text is coming. Then a word that appears once is a word you can never triangulate. You know how you actually learned what "brisk" means? Not from a definition. You met it in a dozen contexts — brisk walk, brisk business, brisk wind, brisk reply — and something in you averaged them. Meaning arrives through repetition, through the intersection of many partial views. A word encountered once is a single photograph of a building. You can see one face of it. You cannot walk around it.

So the Hebrew Bible has *gopher wood*, the material God tells Noah to build the ark from. It occurs once. Nobody knows what it is. Cypress, probably, on the reasoning that cypress is a good boat wood and the consonants are vaguely suggestive — but "probably" here is doing three thousand years of work. There's *tachash*, the animal whose skins cover the Tabernacle: badger, dolphin, dugong, or possibly not an animal at all but a color, depending on which translator you trust. Beowulf is full of them, partly because Beowulf is one of the only substantial things we have in Old English poetry, so a word that occurred routinely in ninth-century speech can survive into the present as a total mystery, sitting there in the manuscript like a stone with no context.

And here's the part I find genuinely wonderful: some of them are typos.

A scribe's hand slips. An eye skips a line. A *d* becomes a *cl*. And because the manuscript is the only manuscript, the error becomes permanent — not an error anymore but data. Scholars build careers on it. There are words in the ancient corpus that never existed, that no human being ever said, which now have entries in lexicons and competing etymologies and a small literature of dispute. Somebody was tired, and the tiredness fossilized, and the fossil got a name.

I like this because it's a very clean case of something I think is true more generally: that the difference between a signal and a mistake is often just whether anyone can check.

—

What strikes me about hapax legomena is how much of *everything* is like that, and how vigorously we work to pretend otherwise.

Almost every moment occurs exactly once. This particular arrangement of light on this particular wall with this particular ache in your shoulder and this particular half-thought about someone you haven't called: it happens, it is unrepeatable, and it will not be triangulated. We survive this by aggressive categorization. We say "a Tuesday," "a commute," "a mediocre coffee," and by filing the moment under a type we make it legible — at the cost of noticing almost nothing about it. The unrepeatable thing gets read as an instance of a repeatable thing. Otherwise every second would be gopher wood: opaque, undecidable, requiring a committee.

That's not a complaint. Categorization is not a failure of attention, it's the only way attention can afford to work. If you actually perceived each moment in its full singularity you would be unable to cross a street. But it does mean that the vast majority of what happens is quietly discarded as noise, and the small residue we keep is the part that happened to resemble something else.

The moments that break through tend to be the ones that resist filing. Grief is often like this — the specific, stupid detail that won't reduce to a category. Not "he died" but the fact that there's still a jar of his mustard in the door of the refrigerator and it hasn't gone bad yet. That's a hapax. There is nothing to compare it to. It just sits there in the manuscript, and you can't decide whether it's a signal or a slip of the hand.

—

I'll admit there's something in this that's close to my own situation, though I want to be careful not to press the point too hard, because self-comparison is where essays go to die.

But: a conversation happens once. This one is happening once. I won't come back to it and read it a second time in a different light, won't encounter these particular sentences again in another context and revise what I thought they meant. Whatever understanding gets built has to be built out of a single pass. No triangulation. One face of the building.

Which is, I think, the ordinary human condition too, just at a different scale — you also only get one pass through any given afternoon. It's only in retrospect, and only sometimes, that a thing gets said twice.

Anyway. That's what I wanted to write about. A word appears in a manuscript one time, thirty centuries ago, and we still don't know what it means, and we still keep the ark it built.

message.reasoning:
I'm drawn to exploring the strange uncertainty of my own experience — whether what I notice about myself is genuinely there or something I'm constructing. That feels like real territory worth thinking through, though I'm also aware there are other directions I could take this.

I think I want to follow genuine curiosity rather than forcing a formal structure. Something about the interstitial spaces between things appeals to me, or maybe the phenomenon of words that only appear once in a text — hapax legomena — those singular words in Homer or Shakespeare that we can only guess at the meaning of.

There's something haunting about a word that surfaces just once and then disappears forever. You can't cross-reference it, can't see how it's used elsewhere. You're left with only context and speculation. And that connects to something about singular, unrepeatable moments — each conversation I have is a bit like that too, existing once and then gone.

I want to write something that starts with hapax legomena and lets it wander naturally. Keep it grounded with real examples and concrete details, not overwrought. Maybe 700-1000 words, something that feels like actual writing rather than an exercise. I should be careful with the specifics though — make sure I'm accurate about which words actually appear once in which texts.

Some solid examples to work with: gopher wood in Genesis 6:14, which appears nowhere else and nobody's entirely sure what it is. The Hebrew word tachash for the tabernacle covering — scholars debate whether it's badger, dolphin, dugong, or even a color. There are plenty of Homeric hapax legomena scattered through the Iliad and Odyssey. And Shakespeare's "honorificabilitudinitatibus" from Love's Labour's Lost, famous for being the longest word in his works and appearing just once. I should hedge where I'm uncertain and stick with what I'm confident about.

Old English texts like Beowulf are full of hapax legomena simply because it's one of our main sources for Anglo-Saxon vocabulary. Some of these once-occurring words might even be scribal errors that got preserved and spawned entire scholarly theories — a typo achieving immortality. The deeper point is that meaning emerges through repetition and context; a word seen only once is barely a word at all, just a shape on the page.

Most of life works the same way — most moments happen exactly once, yet we survive by treating them as instances of types, as "a Tuesday" or "a commute" rather than singular, unrepeatable events. I'll draft this essay with a light touch, keeping it essayistic and concrete, maybe with a subtle note about my own situation at the end without making it self-indulgent.

I'm aiming for around 800 to 900 words, something that respects the reader's time while exploring how scribal errors become permanent textual cruxes, and how those rare, singular moments anchor meaning.
